title: Learn C# from the ground up
hook: C# is a modern language for building reliable software on Microsoft's .NET platform. This track starts with plain English and small examples, then grows into the depth you need for interviews and production work.

blocks.text: C# (pronounced "see sharp") is a statically typed language created by Microsoft. You write human-readable source code in .cs files. A compiler checks your types and turns the source into Intermediate Language (IL) packaged inside assemblies (.dll or .exe files). The Common Language Runtime (CLR) — the .NET run-time host — loads those assemblies, verifies them, and runs your program. The Base Class Library (BCL) is the large set of built-in types you import (lists, strings, HTTP clients, tasks). It is not the language itself — it is the standard library the runtime ships with.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET run-time host that loads assemblies, enforces types, manages memory, and executes your code.
entries.example: A console app or background worker runs inside the CLR, not inside Node.js.

entries.plainDefinition: A CPU-neutral instruction set that .NET compilers emit before the runtime turns it into machine code.
entries.example: Your .cs file becomes IL inside a .dll file.

entries.plainDefinition: The standard set of .NET types for everyday tasks — collections, strings, file I/O, networking, and more.
entries.example: List<T>, string, HttpClient, and Task all come from the BCL.

entries.plainDefinition: The shared type rules every .NET language follows so types from C#, F#, and others can work together.
entries.example: An int in C# maps to the same Common Type System type that other .NET languages understand.

diagram.title: How a C# program runs
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[C# source .cs] --> B[Roslyn compiler]
  B --> C[IL + metadata in assembly]
  C --> D[Common Language Runtime]
  D --> E[Just-In-Time compiler to CPU code]
  E --> F[Your program runs]

snippet.label: A complete C# program
snippet.explanation: Top-level statements compile to a synthesized entry point. Even this tiny file goes through compile → Intermediate Language (IL) → Common Language Runtime (CLR) before anything prints — unlike a JavaScript file that an engine parses directly.

sections.heading: How it differs from JavaScript and TypeScript

blocks.text: If you know JavaScript or TypeScript, C# will feel familiar in syntax (curly braces, semicolons, async/await) but different in what happens at run time. JavaScript is dynamically typed and runs inside engines like V8. TypeScript adds compile-time checking, then erases those types before JavaScript runs. C# keeps types in the assembly as metadata the Common Language Runtime (CLR) enforces. Value types versus reference types, access modifiers, and garbage collection rules are real runtime contracts — not comments that disappear after compile.

blocks.title: C# vs JavaScript and TypeScript at a glance
rows: TypeScript: compile time only; JavaScript: mostly at run time
TypeScript becomes JavaScript; no typed assembly
TypeScript private is erased; JavaScript has no true privacy by default
Promises and async/await over the event loop
Browser or Node.js APIs + npm packages

snippet.label: Types survive after compile
snippet.explanation: The compiler rejects assigning a bool to score. After publish, the Common Language Runtime (CLR) still sees Int32. A TypeScript number would have been erased to an IEEE-754 JavaScript number.

snippet.label: TypeScript types disappear at run time
snippet.explanation: TypeScript interfaces exist only for the checker. C# classes and interfaces are real types in the assembly the Common Language Runtime (CLR) loads.

blocks.text: Modules are numbered in learning order — not by interview popularity. Work through them in sequence unless a time map below fits your schedule. Each module ends with a mind map, a one-screen quick overview, and an interview page for revision.

items.title: Foundations (modules 01–07)
items.body: Program structure, syntax, the type system, classes, object-oriented patterns, exceptions, and null safety. Finish this block before Language Integrated Query (LINQ) or threading.

items.title: Intermediate (modules 08–13)
items.body: Collections, generics, delegates and events, pattern matching, Language Integrated Query (LINQ), and async/await — the code you write in services and workers every week.

items.title: Advanced (modules 14–18)
items.body: Memory and garbage collection, concurrency, assemblies and reflection, Span and unsafe code, then a C# 8–14 recap with performance idioms.

items.title: Revise with mind maps and interview pages
items.body: Use mind maps and interview sections to reinforce what you learned — not as a shortcut around the topic pages.

sections.heading: What you'll build along the way

blocks.text: Every topic uses small, explained code snippets — not toy one-liners. Examples mirror real backend shapes: queue consumers, cache keys, message offload, image disposal, authentication branching, bulk file import, and high-concurrency request paths. You will learn the C# language and .NET fundamentals here. Web frameworks like ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core are covered in separate .NET tracks so this index stays focused on language mastery.

blocks.title: What to expect in each module
blocks.body: Start with a plain-English hook, then glossary terms, diagrams, and step-by-step code. JavaScript and TypeScript comparisons appear wherever they help you transfer what you already know. Interview takeaways at the end of each topic summarize what senior interviewers expect — after the beginner explanation, not instead of it.

snippet.label: Real-world shape: typed handler logic
snippet.explanation: Records, pattern matching, and value semantics show up in production code — not just in syntax drills. You will meet features like this in the modules where they belong, with introducedIn tags on newer C# versions.

stages.title: Foundations (01–07)
stages.summary: Program, syntax, types, members, OOP, exceptions, null safety. Finish this before LINQ or threading.

stages.title: Intermediate (08–13)
stages.summary: Collections, generics, delegates, pattern matching, LINQ, async/await — the code you write in workers every week.

stages.title: Advanced (14–18)
stages.summary: GC, threading, reflection, Span/unsafe, then a C# 8–14 recap and performance idioms.

timeMaps.focus: Still start at foundations. Skim 01–03, then 05 (OOP uniqueness), 06 (using/IDisposable), and 07 (NRT). Do not jump to GC first.
Complete 01–13 with interview pages. That covers daily C# plus async. Leave 14–18 for a third sitting.
All 18 modules in order. Use mind maps and interview pages as revision, not as a substitute for the topic pages.
